rows: The Control of Asbestos Regulations 2012 set minimum standards for protecting workers from asbestos exposure.
The approved code and guidance cover work that disturbs or is likely to disturb asbestos-containing material.
Employers must identify asbestos hazards before work starts and plan suitable controls.
Certain non-licensable asbestos work has notification, medical-surveillance and record-keeping requirements.
Risk assessment must consider the type, condition and likely disturbance of asbestos-containing material.
Work areas and methods must be controlled to reduce fibre release and exposure.
Dutyholders for non-domestic premises must manage asbestos risks and keep information available.
Training, suitable equipment and controlled work practices are core compliance measures.
This is a workplace and premises-management control source, not a direct parcel-level safety measurement.
Applicability depends on building age, material presence, condition, planned work and the identity of the legal dutyholder.
Electrical hazards should be assessed and suitable controls put in place.
Electrical safety guidance covers equipment, installations, maintenance and work near electricity.
Work on electrical systems should be planned and carried out by people with appropriate competence.
Safe isolation is a central control before work on electrical equipment or installations.
Maintenance should keep electrical equipment in a safe condition and address foreseeable deterioration.
Portable appliance testing is one possible maintenance tool; the law requires maintenance based on risk rather than a universal test interval.
Electrical work in potentially explosive locations requires controls suitable for the hazardous atmosphere.
Electrical injuries and ignition risks increase where voltage, equipment condition or work practices are inadequately controlled.
HSE guidance establishes control duties and methods but does not prove the condition of a particular property installation.
Inspection frequency and testing scope depend on equipment type, use, environment and the risk assessment.
The Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005 require employers to prevent or reduce risks from occupational noise.
Employers must assess noise risk and take action to reduce exposure.
Hearing protection is required where exposure cannot be reduced enough by other methods.
The lower exposure action value is 80 dB(A) daily or weekly average.
The upper exposure action value for hearing protection and zones is 85 dB(A).
The exposure limit value is 87 dB(A) after accounting for hearing protection.
Workers at risk require information, instruction and training.
Health surveillance is required where noise exposure creates a risk to hearing.
These thresholds concern occupational exposure and do not represent environmental nuisance noise at a parcel.
Actual exposure depends on duration, task, distance, shielding and use of effective controls.
Employers should protect workers from both hand-arm vibration and whole-body vibration.
Hand-arm vibration can damage blood vessels, nerves and joints.
Whole-body vibration can contribute to back and muscle pain for drivers of some vehicles.
Risk control should begin with eliminating or reducing vibration at source.
Tool and equipment selection should consider vibration emission and suitability for the task.
Exposure duration, trigger time and maintenance condition affect vibration risk.
Workers need information and training on early symptoms and safe work methods.
Health surveillance is appropriate where workers remain at risk from hand-arm vibration.
Vibration duties relate to work exposure and equipment use, not a static parcel-level condition.
Manufacturer emission figures alone may not represent real exposure under site-specific working conditions.
